title: Cite each play extract by speaker and line
statement: Show each extract from a play with its speaker and its line reference, in the numbering of the edition learners see, converting any other numbering first.
example: One cited line is 1.3.208–209 in the act, scene and line numbering students see, but 537–538 in through-line numbers.
detail: A Grade 9 unit's knowledge base gives line references in act, scene and line as printed on the website edition students read, and sets speaker labels in capitals and bold in its reading texts (`g9/sources/1. Act 1 - Knowledge Base - Overview.csv`, lines 135-136). Its quality pass found earlier drafts using the edition's through-line numbers, which match only in the first scene, and converted every later reference, recording the offsets (lines 136 and 143). The first-pass review of the lesson prototype singled out a line citation with its speaker as work to keep, because it teaches the citation convention and names who is speaking, which matters in drama (`g9/sources/Othello_1_Feedback_DevFactory.md`, lines 288 and 354).
against: Another record holds the opposite for any text: point at a text by its words, never its line numbers, since editions number lines differently and a lesson may show none.

evidence.quote: Act.Scene.Line, as printed on folger.edu (for example 1.3.208–209).
Earlier drafts used Folger through-line numbers (FTLN), which only match in 1.1.
All 1.2 and 1.3 references have been converted: 1.2 = FTLN − 206; 1.3 = FTLN − 329.
FTLN references in 1.2 and 1.3 were converted to Act.Scene.Line, which is what students see on folger.edu.
Speaker labels in capitals and bold.
"1.1.171–174 · Iago" teaches the citation convention and names who is speaking.
